title: Gene expression and genetics
unit: A2 (inferred from content; unit number not stated in source)

questions.question: State the sequence of the first four amino acids coded for by the length of DNA shown in the diagram, using the codon table.
questions.answer: Methionine - leucine - isoleucine - tyrosine
steps: Split the DNA into triplets from base 1: ATG | CTC | ATT | TAC | CAT | CGA.
Read each triplet in the table: ATG = methionine, CTC = leucine, ATT = isoleucine, TAC = tyrosine.
Only the first four triplets are needed, so the sequence is Met - Leu - Ile - Tyr.

questions.question: Name the type of each mutation: base 3 becomes C; base 6 becomes number 5 in the sequence; base 9 becomes number 10 in the sequence.
questions.answer: Base 3: substitution. Base 6: deletion. Base 9: insertion.
steps: Base 3 is swapped for C, so one base is replaced by another: a substitution.
Base 6 now has number 5, so a base before it has been lost: a deletion.
Base 9 now has number 10, so an extra base has been added before it: an insertion.
Deletions and insertions shift the reading frame, so every later codon is changed.

questions.question: Explain the possible effects of the substitution, deletion and insertion on the amino acid sequence, using the codon table.
questions.answer: Substitution: one codon changes, so at most one amino acid changes. Deletion and insertion: frameshift, so every codon after the change is altered.
steps: Substitution of base 3 (G to C) changes the first triplet ATG (methionine) to ATC (isoleucine), so only one amino acid is different; the rest of the sequence is unchanged. A substitution could also be silent if the new triplet still codes for the same amino acid (degenerate code).

Deletion (a base lost before base 6) shifts the reading frame, so all triplets after the deletion are read differently. For example, losing base 4 gives Met - Ser - Phe - Thr - Ile instead of Met - Leu - Ile - Tyr - His - Arg.

Insertion (an extra base before base 9) also shifts the reading frame, but triplets before the insertion are unchanged, so Met and Leu are kept and the later amino acids change (for example Met - Leu - Ile - Leu - Pro - Ser).
A frameshift can create a stop codon (TAA, TAG or TGA), giving a shortened polypeptide, or change many amino acids, so the protein folds differently and may not work.
Frameshift mutations are therefore usually more damaging than a single-base substitution.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term gene.
questions.answer: A sequence of DNA bases that codes for a polypeptide (or a functional RNA molecule).
steps: A gene is a section of DNA, not a single base.
The order of its bases is read in triplets called codons.
The sequence codes for one polypeptide chain, which folds into a protein.

questions.question: Explain how mutations in the cystic fibrosis gene result in the disease.
questions.answer: A mutation changes the CFTR base sequence, so the protein has a different amino acid sequence; it folds wrongly and cannot move chloride ions, so mucus becomes thick.
steps: A mutation changes the base sequence of the CFTR gene.
This changes a codon, so a different or missing amino acid is coded for.
The altered amino acid sequence changes how the CFTR protein folds (tertiary structure).
The faulty channel cannot move chloride ions out of cells, so water does not follow by osmosis and the mucus becomes thick and sticky.

questions.question: Suggest why the number of babies born with cystic fibrosis fell after population carrier screening was introduced.
questions.answer: Carriers were identified, so couples who are both carriers could choose prenatal testing or PGD, or choose not to have children, so fewer babies inherit two recessive alleles.
steps: Carrier screening identifies people with one recessive CF allele who show no symptoms.
Two carriers have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child in each pregnancy.
Knowing this, at-risk couples can choose prenatal testing, PGD or not to have children.
Fewer children inherit two copies of the recessive allele, so fewer babies are born with CF.

questions.question: Explain, using the table, how the data show a correlation between the age of the mother and the miscarriage rate.
questions.answer: As age increases, the miscarriage rate of embryos not screened for aneuploidy rises steadily (12.0% to 58.8%), a positive correlation.
steps: In the unscreened column the rate rises with every age band: 12.0% (<35), 16.8, 25.0, 37.9 and 58.8% (>42).
So older women have a higher miscarriage rate: a positive correlation.
The rate is almost five times greater in the oldest group than the youngest (58.8 / 12.0 = 4.9).
Quote figures from at least two age groups to gain the data mark.

questions.question: Explain the conclusions that can be drawn from the data about the causes of miscarriage.
questions.answer: Aneuploidy is a major cause of miscarriage, especially in older women, but it is not the only cause.
steps: Screening removes aneuploid embryos and lowers the miscarriage rate in every age group, so aneuploidy is a cause of miscarriage.
The fall is much larger in older women (58.8% to 17.2% for >42 compared with 12.0% to 11.2% for <35), so aneuploidy accounts for most of the age effect.
Screened embryos still miscarry (11.2 to 17.2%), so other factors also cause miscarriage.
The rate in screened embryos still rises slightly with age (11.2% to 17.2%), so maternal age has a small effect that is independent of aneuploidy.

questions.question: Explain why conclusions made from these miscarriage data may not be valid.
questions.answer: A correlation does not prove causation; other factors were not controlled and the sample may be too small or unrepresentative.
steps: A correlation shows two variables change together, not that one causes the other.
Other factors such as maternal health or lifestyle may also affect miscarriage (confounding variables).
If the sample is small or not representative, the results may not apply to all women.
Without controlled conditions, these other factors cannot be ruled out.

questions.question: Discuss the implications of screening embryos for aneuploidy before implantation.
questions.answer: Fewer miscarriages and better implantation success, but high cost, possible false results and ethical concerns such as discarding embryos.
steps: Only embryos with the correct chromosome number are implanted, so fewer miscarriages are expected.
This can improve success rates and reduce the emotional and physical stress of miscarriage.
Screening needs IVF, which is costly, and tests can give false results.
Ethical concerns include discarding embryos and choosing embryos on criteria other than health.

questions.question: Explain the nature of the genetic code, using the codon table.
questions.answer: The code is a triplet code, degenerate, non-overlapping and universal, with a start codon (ATG) and three stop codons.
steps: Triplet code: three bases (a codon) code for one amino acid; 4^3 = 64 possible codons, more than enough for the 20 amino acids.
Degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon, for example ATA, ATC and ATT all code for isoleucine; only methionine (ATG) and tryptophan (TGG) have a single codon.
Stop codons: TAA, TAG and TGA do not code for an amino acid and end translation; ATG (methionine) is the start codon.
Non-overlapping: each base belongs to only one codon and the sequence is read in order from a fixed start point.
Universal: the same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms.

questions.question: Give the sequence of amino acids coded for by the bases in the antisense strand shown in the diagram.
questions.answer: Tyrosine - arginine - threonine - glycine, then a stop codon (TAG)
steps: The table lists codons as they appear on the sense strand, so first write the complement of the template (antisense) strand ATGGCTTGCCCGATCCTA: TACCGAACGGGCTAGGAT.
Split into triplets: TAC | CGA | ACG | GGC | TAG | GAT.
Read the table: TAC = tyrosine, CGA = arginine, ACG = threonine, GGC = glycine, TAG = stop codon, so translation ends there.
Common error: reading the antisense bases directly (ATG GCT TGC ...) ignores that this strand is the template.

questions.question: Explain the possible effects on a protein of a substitution mutation at the 9th base of the antisense strand, using the codon table.
questions.answer: No effect on the protein: base 9 is the third base of the threonine codon, and any substitution there still codes for threonine (silent mutation).
steps: Base 9 of the template pairs with base 9 of the sense strand, which is the third base of the third codon, ACG (threonine).
Replacing the template base C with A, G or T changes the sense codon to ACT, ACC or ACA.
ACA, ACC, ACG and ACT all code for threonine, because the genetic code is degenerate.
The amino acid sequence (primary structure) is unchanged, so the protein folds and functions normally: a silent mutation.
Only one codon is affected and the reading frame is not shifted, so no other amino acids change.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term gene.
questions.answer: A sequence of DNA bases that codes for a polypeptide (or a functional RNA molecule).
steps: A gene is a section of DNA.
Its base sequence is read as codons.
The codons code for one polypeptide chain.

questions.question: Describe how the two strands of DNA in the double helix of a gene are held together.
questions.answer: By hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A pairs with T (two bonds) and C pairs with G (three bonds).
steps: Each strand has bases attached to a sugar-phosphate backbone.
Bases on opposite strands pair by complementary base pairing: A with T, C with G.
Hydrogen bonds form between each pair, and many of them together hold the strands together.

questions.question: Explain why each codon in the DNA genetic code must contain at least three bases.
questions.answer: Four bases taken two at a time give only 16 codes, which is too few for 20 amino acids; triplets give 64 codes.
steps: DNA has four different bases: A, C, G and T.
Doublets (two bases) give 4 x 4 = 16 different codes.
16 is fewer than the 20 amino acids that need coding.
Triplets give 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 codes, enough for all amino acids and stop codons.

questions.question: A colour-blind father and an unaffected heterozygous mother have a child. Determine the probability that the child is colour blind, using a genetic diagram.
steps: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive: the father is X^bY and the mother is X^BX^b.
The father gives X^b (to daughters) or Y (to sons); the mother gives X^B or X^b, each with probability 1/2.
The four equally likely children are X^BX^b, X^bX^b, X^BY and X^bY, each with probability 1/4.
Colour-blind children are X^bX^b and X^bY, so 2 out of 4 = 1/2.

questions.question: Complete the table of blood clotting components by filling in the names, roles or solubility of each component.
questions.answer: Thromboplastin: converts (activates) prothrombin to thrombin. Row 2: thrombin, soluble. Fibrin: insoluble; forms a mesh of fibres that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot.
steps: Thromboplastin role: released from damaged tissue and platelets; it catalyses (with calcium ions) the conversion of soluble prothrombin into thrombin.
Row 2 name: thrombin, because it is the enzyme that catalyses the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin. Its solubility: soluble.
Fibrin role 1: forms a mesh (network) of long fibres across the wound.
Fibrin role 2: the mesh traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot (scab) that seals the wound and prevents blood loss and entry of pathogens.
Fibrin solubility: insoluble, so the clot stays in place (fibrinogen is its soluble precursor).

questions.question: Explain why more males than females are affected by haemophilia A, which is inherited like red-green colour blindness.
questions.answer: Males have one X chromosome, so one recessive allele causes the disorder; females need two recessive alleles.
steps: The haemophilia A gene is on the X chromosome.
Males (XY) have only one X, so one recessive allele has no second allele to mask it.
Females (XX) need two recessive alleles to show the disorder.
Two recessive alleles in females are much less likely, so fewer females are affected.

questions.question: Draw a genetic diagram showing the genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from two heterozygous brown rabbits (brown dominant, white recessive).
questions.answer: Parents Bb x Bb give 1 BB brown : 2 Bb brown : 1 bb white (3 brown : 1 white).
steps: Brown is dominant (B) and white is recessive (b), so heterozygous rabbits are Bb.
Each parent gives B or b with probability 1/2 (meiosis separates the alleles).
The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb.
Offspring: 1 BB and 2 Bb are brown, 1 bb is white.

questions.question: From 284 baby rabbits of heterozygous pairs, calculate the expected numbers of homozygous brown, heterozygous brown and white rabbits.
questions.answer: Homozygous brown 71; heterozygous brown 142; white 71.
steps: The expected ratio from Bb x Bb is 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, so the probabilities are 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.
Homozygous brown (BB): 1/4 x 284 = 71.
Heterozygous brown (Bb): 1/2 x 284 = 142.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term genotype.
questions.answer: The alleles an organism carries for a particular gene (its genetic makeup).
steps: Genotype describes which alleles an individual has for a gene.
Phenotype is the observable characteristic that results from the genotype.

questions.question: State the probability that the next tiger born to these two parents will be female.
steps: Females are XX and males are XY.
The father always gives an X or a Y; the mother always gives an X.
So each birth has a 1 in 2 chance of being female.

questions.question: Determine the expected phenotypic ratio of orange to white tigers born to the parents in the pedigree, using a genetic diagram.
questions.answer: 3 orange : 1 white (both parents carry the recessive allele: Oo x Oo gives OO, Oo, Oo, oo).
steps: Both parents are orange but they have white offspring, so white is recessive; let O = orange (dominant) and o = white.
Each parent must be heterozygous (Oo), since each passes o to a white (oo) cub.
Gametes: O or o from each parent. Punnett square: OO, Oo, Oo, oo.
Three genotypes (OO, Oo, Oo) give orange and one (oo) gives white, so the expected ratio is 3 orange : 1 white.

questions.question: Calculate the incidence of white tigers in captivity, given 200 white tigers out of approximately 6000 Bengal tigers.
steps: Incidence = number of white tigers divided by total tigers.
This is about 1 in 30 tigers in captivity.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in the diameter of the trachea lumen in a person with cystic fibrosis, measured between X and Y on each diagram.
questions.answer: About 33% decrease (accept roughly 30 to 37%)
steps: Measure X to Y on each diagram, using the same scale: without cystic fibrosis about 149 units; with cystic fibrosis about 100 units (on the page image; a ruler in cm gives the same ratio).
Decrease = 149 - 100 = 49 units.
Percentage decrease = 49 / 149 x 100 = 33%.
Working in the same units for both diagrams and dividing by the original (without cystic fibrosis) value is what gains the marks.

questions.question: Explain why cystic fibrosis causes the differences shown in the trachea diagrams.
questions.answer: Faulty CFTR causes thick mucus that builds up and narrows the lumen; infection then inflames the airway muscle, narrowing it further.
steps: A mutated CFTR gene makes a faulty chloride ion channel protein, so chloride ions are not moved out of the airway cells.
Less water moves out of the cells by osmosis, so the mucus is thick and sticky and forms a thick layer on the airway wall (the mucus layer in the diagram).
Cilia cannot move thick mucus up and out of the trachea, so it accumulates and narrows the lumen.
Trapped bacteria and other pathogens cause repeated infection and an immune response (inflammation).
The muscle in the trachea wall becomes inflamed and swollen (thicker), which narrows the lumen even more, making breathing difficult.

questions.question: Explain how identifying carriers by genetic screening could have contributed to the downward trend in babies with cystic fibrosis.
questions.answer: Carriers are identified and can make informed reproductive choices, so fewer children inherit two CF alleles.
steps: Screening identifies carriers (heterozygotes) who have one CF allele and no symptoms.
Couples who are both carriers know they have a 1 in 4 risk in each pregnancy.
They can use prenatal testing, PGD or choose not to have a child, which avoids affected births.
Fewer affected children are born, so the number of babies with CF falls.

questions.question: Describe the ethical issues relating to genetic screening.
questions.answer: Privacy of genetic data, discrimination, psychological stress, moral views on abortion, informed consent and false results.
steps: Genetic information is personal, so privacy and confidentiality must be protected.
Results may lead to discrimination by employers or insurers.
Carriers or parents may face stress, and there may be pressure to terminate pregnancies.
Screening must be voluntary with informed consent, and false results can cause harm.

questions.question: Explain why a mutation in the CFTR gene results in very thick, sticky mucus.
questions.answer: The mutated CFTR protein cannot move chloride ions out of cells, so water does not follow by osmosis and the mucus becomes thick.
steps: A mutation changes the CFTR gene, so the protein has an altered shape or is absent.
CFTR is a chloride ion channel, so chloride ions cannot leave the cell.
Water does not follow the chloride ions by osmosis, so the mucus is less watery.
The mucus becomes very thick and sticky.

questions.question: Explain why very thick, sticky mucus results in the health problems shown in the diagram for a female with cystic fibrosis.
questions.answer: Thick mucus blocks tubes: in the lungs it blocks airways and causes infections; in the pancreas it blocks enzyme release; in the reproductive tract it blocks the movement of gametes.
steps: Breathing difficulties: thick mucus blocks the airways and cannot be moved by cilia, so air flow and gas exchange are reduced.
Mucus also traps bacteria in the lungs, which leads to repeated infections and inflammation.
Problems absorbing nutrients: mucus blocks the pancreatic duct, so digestive enzymes (lipase, protease, amylase) cannot reach the small intestine.
Food is therefore not fully digested, and mucus on the gut wall also reduces absorption, so nutrients are not absorbed.
Infertility: thick mucus blocks the oviducts or thickens cervical mucus, so sperm cannot reach the egg and fertilisation is less likely.

questions.question: Which is the change in chloride ion concentration in sweat when CFTR function falls from 100% to 18%? Options: A 15, B 35, C 40, D 80 mmol dm^-3.
questions.answer: C: 40 mmol dm^-3
steps: Read the graph at 100% CFTR function: chloride concentration about 20 mmol dm^-3.
At 18% CFTR function the point is at 60 mmol dm^-3.
Change = 60 - 20 = 40 mmol dm^-3, which is option C.

questions.question: Explain how the graph of chloride concentration against CFTR function provides evidence that cystic fibrosis results from different mutations in the CFTR gene.
questions.answer: People with cystic fibrosis have a range of CFTR function (3 to 18%) and different sweat chloride levels, so the CFTR protein is altered in different ways by different mutations.
steps: Individuals with cystic fibrosis have 18% function or less, but the graph shows different values (about 3%, 10% and 18%).
Their sweat chloride concentrations differ (about 100, 73 and 60 mmol dm^-3).
Different mutations change the base sequence and amino acid sequence differently, so the protein folds differently and keeps different amounts of function.
If there were only one mutation, all people with cystic fibrosis would show the same level of function.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term mutation.
questions.answer: A change in the base sequence of DNA (genetic material).
steps: A mutation is a random change in the genetic material.
It alters the base sequence of DNA, which may change a protein.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term correlation.
questions.answer: A relationship between two variables in which a change in one is associated with a change in the other.
steps: A correlation is a statistical link between two variables.
It can be positive (both rise) or negative (one rises as the other falls).
It does not by itself show that one variable causes the other.

questions.question: Describe the correlations shown by the graphs of skin cancer incidence in males and females from 2000 to 2005.
questions.answer: Incidence of skin cancer rises with age in both sexes (positive correlation), and it also rises from 2000 to 2005.
steps: Age: for every year shown, incidence increases as age increases, slowly at first and very steeply after 50 (a positive correlation), in both males and females.
Year: incidence increases from 2000 to 2005 at each age; for males over 80 it rises from about 70 to about 220 per 100 000, and for females over 80 from about 35 to about 105.
Both correlations are positive. Quote figures from the graphs to support them.

questions.question: Suggest a reason for each of the correlations shown by the skin cancer graphs.
questions.answer: Age: longer cumulative exposure to UV and more mutations accumulate in older people. Year: UV exposure or detection of skin cancer increased over 2000 to 2005.
steps: With age, people have had more years of exposure to UV light, so more mutations have built up in skin cells (and DNA repair and immune surveillance become less effective).
Over the years 2000 to 2005, exposure to UV may have increased (more sunbathing, tanning beds, thinner ozone layer).
Alternatively, more screening and awareness of skin cancer leads to more cases being diagnosed, or the population has aged.

questions.question: Criticise the design of the study of the incidence of emphysema in smokers and non-smokers, using the table.
questions.answer: Study too small, with unequal and very few smokers, age and other variables not controlled, and the results are inconsistent between the sexes.
steps: Sample size is small (25 males, 25 females) and only 5 male and 6 female smokers, so results may not be reliable or representative.
Smokers and non-smokers are very unequal in number (5 v 20 males, 6 v 19 females), which makes comparison between the groups unreliable.
Results are inconsistent between the sexes: 1 of 5 male smokers (20%) but 6 of 6 female smokers (100%) had emphysema, so it is not clear that smoking is the only cause.

Age range is wide (32 to 77 years) and other variables (pollution, occupation, family history, how many cigarettes and for how long) are not controlled or recorded, so confounding factors are possible.
No statistical test was applied, so it is not known whether the difference is significant; a correlation does not prove smoking causes emphysema, and smoking status may be self-reported.

questions.question: Which polysaccharide does the liver store when blood glucose is too high? A amylopectin, B cellulose, C glycogen, D starch.
questions.answer: C glycogen.
steps: The liver stores excess glucose as glycogen, a branched polymer of glucose.
Amylopectin and starch are plant stores, and cellulose is a structural polysaccharide.

questions.question: Which pair of carbohydrates can be digested to release glucose? A fructose and sucrose, B fructose and galactose, C galactose and lactose, D lactose and sucrose.
questions.answer: D lactose and sucrose.
steps: Sucrose is glucose plus fructose, so it releases glucose on digestion.
Lactose is glucose plus galactose, so it also releases glucose.
Fructose and galactose do not contain glucose.

questions.question: There are 415 million people with diabetes and 46% are undiagnosed. Calculate the number of people with undiagnosed diabetes.
questions.answer: 190.9 million (about 191 million).
steps: 46% as a decimal is 0.46.
415 million x 0.46 = 190.9 million people.

questions.question: Explain why doctors are more likely to screen individuals once they develop diabetes than use methods such as prenatal testing.
questions.answer: Diabetes is multifactorial (genes plus lifestyle), so a prenatal test cannot predict it reliably; screening after symptoms confirms the type needed for treatment.
steps: Diabetes, especially Type II, is influenced by many genes and by environment and lifestyle, not by one gene.
A prenatal test can show only a genetic risk, not whether diabetes will develop.
Once symptoms appear, a test can confirm the diagnosis and type.
Type I and Type II need different treatments, so a correct diagnosis is essential.

questions.question: Complete the pedigree diagram: individual 7 as a male taster, individual 8 as a male non-taster, individual 9 as a female taster.
questions.answer: Individual 7: unshaded square (male taster); individual 8: filled (black) square (male non-taster); individual 9: unshaded circle (female taster).
steps: Use the key: squares are males and circles are females; unshaded means taster and filled (black) means non-taster.
7 is a male taster, so draw an unshaded square at the end of the line next to 6.
8 is a male non-taster, so draw a filled square; 9 is a female taster, so draw an unshaded circle, both joined below the parents.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a gene and an allele, using the PTC tasting example.
questions.answer: A gene is a section of DNA coding for the bitter-taste receptor; an allele is one of the different versions of that gene (e.g. taster or non-taster).
steps: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for one characteristic, here the bitter-taste receptor.
Alleles are the different forms of the same gene.
The taster and non-taster versions are two alleles of the PTC gene.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a genotype and a phenotype, using the PTC tasting example.
questions.answer: Genotype is the alleles an individual has (e.g. TT, Tt or tt); phenotype is the observable trait (taster or non-taster).
steps: Genotype is the combination of alleles an individual carries.
Phenotype is the observable characteristic produced by the genotype.
For example, a Tt individual has the genotype Tt and is a taster.

questions.question: Explain which allele is dominant, using the information in the pedigree diagram.
questions.answer: Taster is dominant: tasters 1 and 2 have a non-taster daughter (6), so both carry the recessive non-taster allele, which is masked in them.
steps: Individuals 1 and 2 are both tasters but they have a non-taster child (individual 6).
The non-taster allele must therefore be present, but hidden, in both parents, so it is recessive.
So the taster allele is the dominant one: it is expressed even when the non-taster allele is also present (parents Tt and Tt, child tt).

questions.question: Explain why this gene is unlikely to be located on the X chromosome, using the pedigree diagram.
questions.answer: The non-taster daughter (6) has a taster father (1); if the gene were X-linked recessive her father would also have to be a non-taster.
steps: Individual 6 is a female non-taster, so (if non-tasting were recessive and X-linked) she would have two recessive alleles on her X chromosomes.
She must have inherited one X chromosome from her father, individual 1, so he would also carry the recessive allele and be a non-taster.
Individual 1 is a taster, so this pattern does not fit X-linked inheritance and the gene is more likely to be on an autosome.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a gene and an allele, using feather colour in chickens to illustrate.
questions.answer: A gene controls feather colour; alleles are the different forms of that gene, such as black (B) and white (W).
steps: The feather colour gene is a section of DNA that codes for the colour pigment.
Alleles are different forms of the same gene, such as the black allele B and the white allele W.
Each chicken carries two alleles for the gene.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a genotype and a phenotype, using feather colour to illustrate.
questions.answer: Genotype is the alleles (e.g. BW for speckled); phenotype is the feather colour seen (speckled).
steps: Genotype is the pair of alleles the chicken carries, such as BW.
Phenotype is the feather colour produced by the genotype, such as speckled.
Because the alleles are codominant, both black and white show in BW chickens.

questions.question: A black chicken was mated with a speckled chicken and they had 25 chicks. Determine the expected number of speckled chicks, using a genetic diagram.
questions.answer: 12.5 (about 12 or 13 speckled chicks).
steps: Black chickens are BB; speckled chickens are BW because the alleles are codominant.
The cross BB x BW gives gametes B from the black parent and B or W from the speckled parent.
Offspring: 1/2 BB (black) and 1/2 BW (speckled).
Expected speckled chicks = 1/2 x 25 = 12.5.

questions.question: Name the statistical test used to analyse the expected and actual numbers of chicks.
questions.answer: Chi-squared test.
steps: Observed and expected counts in categories are compared with a chi-squared test.
It tests whether the difference is due to chance (null hypothesis).

questions.question: Complete the table of expected numbers of speckled, white and black chicks from 480 chicks.
questions.answer: (O - E): speckled +3, white +5, black -8. (O - E)^2 / E: speckled 0.0375, white 0.208, black 0.533.

questions.question: Calculate the chi-squared value for the chick data.
questions.answer: chi-squared = 0.78 (0.779)
steps: Add the three (O - E)^2 / E values from the table.
To 2 s.f. the chi-squared value is 0.78.

questions.question: Explain how a critical value table could be used to accept or reject the null hypothesis for this experiment.
questions.answer: Compare the calculated chi-squared value with the critical value at the correct degrees of freedom and significance level; reject the null hypothesis if the calculated value is larger.
steps: Find the degrees of freedom (number of categories minus 1).
Read the critical value at the 0.05 significance level for that degrees of freedom.
If the calculated chi-squared value is larger, reject the null hypothesis (a significant difference).
If it is smaller, accept the null hypothesis (the difference is due to chance).

questions.question: Which is the correct statement about the formation of glycogen? Options: A alpha glucose molecules join together by a condensation reaction, B alpha glucose molecules join together by a hydrolysis reaction, C beta glucose molecules join together by a condensation reaction, D beta glucose molecules join together by a hydrolysis reaction.
questions.answer: A (alpha glucose molecules join together by condensation reactions, which remove water).
steps: Glycogen is a polymer built from alpha glucose, not beta glucose, so C and D are wrong.
Joining monomers into a polymer removes water, which is a condensation reaction.
Hydrolysis adds water and breaks polymers down, so B is wrong and A is correct.

questions.question: Name the bond that joins two glucose molecules together.
questions.answer: Glycosidic bond.
steps: Two glucose molecules are joined by a 1,4-glycosidic bond.
The bond forms by condensation, with water removed.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of glycogen relates to its role as an energy storage molecule.
questions.answer: Glycogen is a compact, insoluble, branched polymer, so it stores much glucose without affecting osmosis, and its many ends allow quick glucose release.
steps: Glycogen is a polymer of many glucose units, which stores a large amount of energy in a small space.
It is compact and insoluble, so it does not change the water potential of cells.
The branches give many free ends where enzymes can act at once.
Glucose can therefore be released quickly when energy is needed.

questions.question: Between one in 20 000 and one in 25 000 babies are born with glycogen storage disease (GSD), and about 25% of GSD patients have Von Gierke disease. Estimate the number of babies born each year with Von Gierke disease in a country with 3.8 million births.
questions.answer: About 38 to 48 babies a year (midpoint about 43).
steps: Von Gierke is 25% of these: 0.25 x 152 = 38 and 0.25 x 190 = 47.5.
So the estimate is about 38 to 48 babies, roughly 43.

questions.question: Suggest why the majority of babies with Von Gierke disease are born to parents who are not affected.
questions.answer: The disease is recessive, so unaffected parents are usually carriers, and carriers are far more common than affected people.
steps: Von Gierke disease is inherited as a recessive allele.
Unaffected parents can be heterozygous carriers, each with one recessive allele.
Carriers are much more common in the population than people with the disease.
So most affected children come from two unaffected carrier parents.

questions.question: Which are the products of lactose digestion? A fructose and galactose, B fructose and glucose, C galactose and glucose, D glucose and glucose.
questions.answer: C galactose and glucose.
steps: Lactose is a disaccharide made of glucose and galactose.
Lactase hydrolyses the glycosidic bond, releasing one glucose and one galactose.

questions.question: Explain how the three-dimensional structure of lactase affects its mechanism of action.
questions.answer: Its active site has a shape complementary to lactose, so only lactose binds; a change in shape means the substrate no longer fits.
steps: The tertiary structure of lactase forms an active site with a specific shape.
Lactose binds to the active site because its shape is complementary (lock and key or induced fit).
The enzyme-substrate complex lowers the activation energy so lactose is hydrolysed.
If the 3D shape changes (e.g. denaturation), the active site changes and lactose cannot bind.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage of using immobilised lactase rather than free lactase.
questions.answer: The enzyme can be reused and is easily removed, so the milk is not contaminated with enzyme.
steps: Immobilised enzymes stay in the beads, so they do not mix with the milk.
Because the enzyme is not used up, it can be reused, which lowers cost.

questions.question: Explain the effects of pH on the activity of free lactase and immobilised lactase, using the table.
questions.answer: Both enzymes work best near pH 5 and lose activity at higher and lower pH; immobilised lactase is less affected, and is still active at pH 3 where free lactase is not.
steps: Both enzymes have highest activity near pH 5 (free 94 a.u., immobilised 98 a.u.), the optimum pH.

Away from the optimum, extra H+ or OH- ions break ionic and hydrogen bonds in the tertiary structure, changing the shape of the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and activity falls (free lactase falls to 28 a.u. at pH 8).
At pH 2 both enzymes are denatured (0 a.u.), but at pH 3 immobilised lactase is still active (38 a.u.) while free lactase is not (0 a.u.).

At pH 5 to 8 immobilised lactase has equal or higher activity than free lactase (for example 76 v 63 a.u. at pH 6), because being enclosed in the beads helps hold the enzyme in shape, so it is more tolerant of changes in pH.

questions.question: Suggest how the rate of activity of lactase could be measured, including appropriate units.
questions.answer: Measure the amount of glucose (or galactose) produced per unit time, e.g. in mmol per minute (mmol min^-1).
steps: Lactase hydrolyses lactose, so the product glucose builds up over time.
Measure glucose concentration at set times, e.g. with glucose test strips or a biosensor.
Rate = amount of product formed / time, giving units such as mmol min^-1.

questions.question: Suggest why most people with congenital lactose intolerance are found in one country.
questions.answer: The recessive allele is common in that population, through the founder effect or inbreeding.
steps: CLI is a rare recessive genetic disorder.
A founder population or inbreeding can concentrate a recessive allele in that group.
Individuals who inherit two copies are then more common in that country.

questions.question: Which best describes a mutation? A change in the amino acid sequence in DNA, B change in the amino acid sequence in a protein, C change in the base sequence in DNA, D change in the base sequence in a protein.
questions.answer: C a change in the base sequence in DNA.
steps: A mutation is a change to the base sequence of DNA.
Amino acid changes in proteins are a result of mutations, not the definition.

questions.question: Name two types of mutation.
questions.answer: Any two of: substitution, insertion, deletion.
steps: A substitution replaces one base with another.
An insertion adds a base and a deletion removes a base (both cause frameshifts).

questions.topic: Cancer Cases By Age And Sex
questions.question: Describe the effect of age and sex on the number of cases of one type of cancer, using the graph.
questions.answer: Cases rise with age in both sexes; females have more cases up to about 59 years, after which males have more and the rise is steeper.
steps: Age: the number of cases increases with age for both males and females (about 3600 for males and 2250 for females per 100 000 at 90 years).
Females: cases start at about 20 years and rise fairly steadily; they are higher than males in younger groups (about 450 v 200 per 100 000 at 40 years).
Males: cases start at about 30 years but rise more steeply, so the lines cross at about 59 years (about 950 per 100 000), after which males have more cases than females.

questions.question: Give the seventh triplet code in the beta-globin gene of a person with sickle cell disease, using the table of bases and amino acids.
questions.answer: GUG
steps: The seventh triplet in the healthy gene is GAG, which codes for Glu.
Sickle cell disease replaces Glu with Val; in the table Val is coded by GUG (second triplet).
So the middle base A is replaced by U (GAG becomes GUG), a single base change.

questions.question: Name the type of mutation that causes sickle cell disease.
questions.answer: Substitution (a point mutation changing one base).
steps: Sickle cell disease is caused by one base changed in the beta-globin gene.
A single base being replaced is a substitution mutation.

questions.question: Explain why replacing hydrophilic Glu with hydrophobic Val causes haemoglobin molecules to stick together.
questions.answer: Val is hydrophobic and sits on the surface, so it binds to hydrophobic patches on other haemoglobin molecules, and they stick together.
steps: Glu is polar and hydrophilic, so it stays dissolved and interacts with water on the surface.
Val is hydrophobic (non-polar), so it is pushed out of the water and onto the surface.
The hydrophobic Val groups on one haemoglobin molecule bind to hydrophobic patches on others.
The haemoglobin molecules therefore clump together into fibres.

questions.question: In 2020 about 140 million babies were born and about 305 800 had sickle cell disease. Estimate the ratio of babies with the disease to those without it.
questions.answer: About 1 : 457.
steps: Babies without the disease = 140 000 000 - 305 800 = 139 694 200.

questions.question: Calculate the largest difference in p50 values between people with and without sickle cell disease, using the oxygen dissociation curves.
questions.answer: 3.4 kPa
steps: p50 is the partial pressure of oxygen at 50% saturation; read across from 50% to the edges of each shaded area.
People without sickle cell disease: p50 from about 4.4 to 4.9 kPa. People with sickle cell disease: about 5.7 to 7.8 kPa.
Largest difference = highest value for sickle cell disease - lowest value for people without = 7.8 - 4.4 = 3.4 kPa.
Give to 1 decimal place, matching the precision to which the graph can be read (accept 3.3 to 3.5).

questions.question: Identify two conclusions, other than the p50 difference, that can be made from the oxygen dissociation graph.
questions.answer: Sickle cell group shows a wider range of values (more variation); at the same partial pressure of oxygen its haemoglobin is less saturated.
steps: Conclusion 1: the sickle cell disease band is much wider than the non-sickle band (at 50% saturation about 2.1 kPa wide v 0.5 kPa), so there is more variation between people with the disease.

Conclusion 2: at any given partial pressure of oxygen the haemoglobin of people with sickle cell disease is less saturated (for example about 21 to 39% v 52 to 60% at 5 kPa), so it has a lower affinity for oxygen and the curve is shifted to the right.

Other acceptable points: both groups show S-shaped curves, saturation rises as partial pressure of oxygen rises, and the people with sickle cell disease need a higher partial pressure to approach full saturation.

questions.question: A red blood cell lifespan of 11 days in sickle cell disease is 9.17% of a healthy cell's lifespan. Calculate the healthy lifespan to the nearest day.
questions.answer: 120 days.
steps: Healthy lifespan = 11 / 0.0917 = 119.96.
To the nearest day this is 120 days.

questions.question: Explain why the changes in haemoglobin structure and red blood cell shape could result in death in sickle cell disease.
questions.answer: Sickled cells block capillaries and carry less oxygen, so tissues and organs are starved of oxygen and fail.
steps: Abnormal haemoglobin molecules stick together and form fibres inside the cell.
The cells become sickle-shaped and less elastic, so they get stuck in capillaries.
Blocked capillaries and fewer working cells mean less oxygen reaches the tissues.
Tissues, especially vital organs, are damaged and may fail, causing death.

questions.question: In 2018 in the UK there were 541 589 deaths, 166 800 caused by cancer. Calculate the ratio of cancer deaths to non-cancer deaths, to two decimal places.
steps: To two decimal places the ratio is 0.45 : 1.

questions.question: Name two other types of mutation shown in the chart of cancers caused by different mutations.
questions.answer: Insertion and deletion (inversion, duplication or translocation are also acceptable)
steps: The chart shows three types of substitution and a group labelled other types of mutation.
The other types of gene mutation are insertion (a base added) and deletion (a base lost).
Larger chromosome changes such as inversion, duplication and translocation would also gain the mark.

questions.question: Estimate the percentage of cancers caused by type 3 substitution mutations, from the chart.
questions.answer: About 64% (accept 60 to 68%)
steps: Type 3 is the largest segment, running clockwise from the top for about 230 degrees of the circle.
Percentage = 230 / 360 x 100 = 64%.
Check: type 1 is about 23%, type 2 about 4% and other types about 8%; 64 + 23 + 4 + 8 = 99%, allowing for rounding.

questions.question: Explain how a substitution mutation can change the DNA and mRNA but not the protein made from the gene.
questions.answer: The base change alters one codon, but the new codon still codes for the same amino acid because the genetic code is degenerate.
steps: The substitution changes one base, so the DNA base sequence changes.
The mRNA is transcribed from it, so the mRNA codon is also changed.
Because the genetic code is degenerate, more than one codon can code for the same amino acid.
The new codon still codes for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged (a silent mutation).

questions.question: What is the probability that couple 1 and 2 have a fourth child who is a male affected by PKU? Options: A 0.000, B 0.125, C 0.250, D 0.500.
steps: Individuals 3 and 4 are affected sons of unaffected parents 1 and 2, so PKU is recessive and both parents are carriers (Pp x Pp).
Probability of an affected child (pp) = 1/4.
Probability the child is male = 1/2.
Probability of an affected male = 1/4 x 1/2 = 1/8 = 0.125, which is option B.

questions.question: Discuss the extent to which the PKU pedigree diagram can be used to identify the genotypes of all members of the family.
questions.answer: Genotypes are certain only for the affected (pp) individuals 3 and 4 and their parents 1 and 2 (Pp); individuals 5 to 9 could be PP or Pp.
steps: PKU is recessive: unaffected parents 1 and 2 have affected children (3 and 4), so the allele is hidden in the parents.
Affected individuals 3 and 4 must be homozygous recessive (pp).
Parents 1 and 2 each passed a recessive allele to their affected sons, so both are heterozygous carriers (Pp).
Individual 5 is unaffected and the child of two carriers, so could be PP or Pp (probability 2/3 of Pp); the pedigree cannot show which.
Individual 6 is an unaffected outsider with no family history shown, so could be PP or Pp. Children 7, 8 and 9 are unaffected and each could be PP or Pp, as only 5 and 6 are unknown.
So the pedigree identifies the genotypes of only 1, 2, 3 and 4; the others could only be found by genetic testing or by more offspring.

questions.question: Complete the table giving the number of people with red-green colour blindness in India and the percentage in Malaysia.
steps: India: number = 5.2 / 100 x 1380 = 71.76 million, about 71.8 million.
Malaysia: percentage = 1.024 / 32 x 100 = 3.2%.
Check using Japan: 3.024 / 126 x 100 = 2.4%, which matches the table.

questions.question: The percentage of males in Malaysia who are colour blind is 6.7% and of females 0.4%. Calculate the ratio of colour blind males to females.
Explain why the percentage of colour blind males is greater than the percentage of colour blind females.
questions.answer: Males have one X chromosome, so one recessive allele causes colour blindness; females need two recessive alleles, which is much rarer.
steps: The gene is on the X chromosome; males are XY and have only one X.
A single recessive allele on that X is expressed in males because the Y has no gene for colour vision.
Females (XX) need two recessive alleles, so they must be homozygous to be colour blind.
The chance of two recessive alleles is much lower than one, so fewer females are affected.

questions.question: Explain why the inheritance of blood type shown in the pedigree is an example of codominance.
questions.answer: In a heterozygote both alleles are fully expressed, so both antigens appear and neither allele is masked.
steps: Codominant alleles are both expressed in a heterozygous individual.
Individuals 1 and 2 are homozygous for different blood types.
Their heterozygous child shows both antigens, so neither allele is dominant or recessive.

questions.question: Determine the ratio of possible blood type phenotypes of the children of individuals 3 and 4, drawing a genetic diagram.
questions.answer: 1 blood group M : 2 blood group MN : 1 blood group N
steps: Individuals 3 and 4 are both blood group MN, so both are heterozygous: L^M L^N (the alleles are codominant).
Gametes from each parent: L^M or L^N.
Punnett square: L^M L^M, L^M L^N, L^M L^N, L^N L^N.
Phenotypes: 1 group M : 2 group MN : 1 group N (probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4).

questions.question: Explain how the alleles present in individual 3 result in the proteins found on the surfaces of his red blood cells, using the diagram of red blood cells.
questions.answer: Individual 3 is heterozygous (L^M L^N); both alleles are expressed, so he makes both protein M and protein N on his red blood cells.
steps: Individual 3 is MN, so he inherited the M allele from his father (individual 1) and the N allele from his mother (individual 2).
Each allele is transcribed and translated into a different protein: the M allele codes for protein M and the N allele codes for protein N.
The alleles are codominant, so neither masks the other and both proteins are made and placed in the red blood cell membrane.

questions.question: Discuss the possible effects that a mutation in one of the genes coding for this blood type could have on the phenotype of individual 3.
questions.answer: The effect depends on the mutation: it may be silent, change the antigen shape, or stop the protein being made, so the blood group phenotype may change.
steps: A substitution may code for the same amino acid (silent), so the phenotype is unchanged.
A substitution that changes an amino acid can alter the antigen shape, so the blood group may change.
A deletion or insertion shifts the reading frame, so a non-functional protein or none is made.
Loss of the antigen from one allele may be hidden or only partly changed if the other allele is still expressed in a heterozygote.

questions.question: Explain why the change in mean FEV1 was used in this investigation of a three-drug combination for cystic fibrosis.
questions.answer: FEV1 is a measure of lung function, and the change in mean FEV1 shows the effect of the treatment on each group.
steps: FEV1 is the volume of air forcibly exhaled in one second, a measure of lung function.
A change in mean FEV1 shows whether the treatment improved lung function.
Using the change compares the starting and finishing values for each group fairly.

questions.question: Explain why the results of this investigation do not show that the three-drug treatment is more effective than using each drug on its own.
questions.answer: Each drug alone was not tested in the study, so there is no comparison to show the combination is better.
steps: The study compared the combination with a different group, not with each drug given alone.
Without a group taking each drug separately, the extra benefit of the combination cannot be shown.

questions.question: Suggest why a combination of drugs could be more effective in treating cystic fibrosis than each drug used alone.
questions.answer: Different drugs can target different faults in the CFTR protein, so their effects add together or work together.
steps: Different mutations in CFTR cause different faults in the protein.
Each drug may correct a different fault (e.g. folding or channel opening).
Together they can work at more than one point, giving a larger total effect.

questions.question: Explain why a healthy couple might choose a prenatal test for PKU, drawing a genetic diagram.
questions.answer: Both parents are carriers (Pp), so each child has a 1 in 4 chance of PKU (pp); prenatal testing shows whether the embryo is affected.
steps: PKU is autosomal recessive; a healthy couple may both be carriers (Pp).
Cross Pp x Pp gives PP, Pp, Pp and pp in a ratio of 1 : 2 : 1.
Each pregnancy has a 1/4 chance of an affected child (pp).
Prenatal testing can show whether the embryo has PKU, so the couple can make an informed choice.

questions.question: Discuss the responses of women to three questions about screening for four genetic disorders, using the graph and table.
questions.answer: Most women would accept a blood test, fewer an amniocentesis, and far fewer termination, which depends strongly on how severe the disorder is.
steps: Blood test: very high for every disorder (about 94 to 98%), because it is non-invasive and carries no risk to the baby.
Amniocentesis: lower than the blood test for every disorder (about 64 to 72%) and similar across disorders; it is invasive and carries a small risk of miscarriage.
Termination: much lower and varies widely: highest for disorder A (about 62%), then D (about 41%), B (about 20%) and C (about 10%).

Link to the table: more women would terminate when the disorder is severe or sometimes lethal (A) than when it is treatable with a normal or near-normal life (B and C); D (intellectual disability) is in between.
Fewer women would terminate than have amniocentesis, because a test result can also be used to prepare for the child rather than to end the pregnancy.

Limitations: only opinions of women who had recently had healthy babies, so they may not reflect women in families affected by the disorders; what they say they would do may differ from what they would actually do.

questions.question: Explain how human lungs are adapted for rapid gas exchange.
questions.answer: Many thin-walled alveoli give a large surface area, and a rich capillary network keeps a steep concentration gradient.
steps: The alveoli give a large surface area for diffusion.
Alveolar walls are one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short.
A dense capillary network maintains a steep concentration gradient for oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Ventilation keeps the air in the alveoli fresh with high oxygen concentration.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term allele.
questions.answer: An alternative form of a gene, found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
steps: A gene can exist in different versions.
These versions are alleles and occupy the same position (locus) on homologous chromosomes.

questions.question: The F508 mutation gives a CFTR protein with one missing amino acid. Explain how this results in a non-functioning protein.
questions.answer: Losing one amino acid changes the primary structure, so the protein folds incorrectly and cannot work as a chloride channel.
steps: Three bases (one codon) are deleted, so one amino acid is missing from the polypeptide.
The primary structure changes, which alters the hydrogen and ionic bonds in the chain.
The protein folds into the wrong tertiary shape.
The misfolded CFTR cannot act as a chloride channel, so it does not function.

questions.question: Explain why people with cystic fibrosis may develop lung infections.
questions.answer: Thick mucus cannot be cleared by cilia, so bacteria are trapped and multiply in the airways.
steps: Faulty CFTR means chloride and water do not pass out, so mucus is thick and sticky.
Cilia cannot move this mucus, so it is not cleared from the airways.
Trapped bacteria grow in the warm, moist mucus and cause infection.
The inflammatory response then damages the lungs further.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the genotype and phenotype of individual 1 in the pedigree?
questions.answer: B: genotype Cc, unaffected heterozygous
steps: The allele for CMT (c) is recessive, so an affected person is cc.
Individual 1 is unaffected but has an affected son (individual 4, cc), so he must have passed on a c allele.
Individual 1 is therefore heterozygous (Cc) and unaffected: row B.

questions.question: Which allele combinations could individual 3 have? A CC only, B cc only, C CC or cc, D CC or Cc.
questions.answer: D: CC or Cc
steps: Individual 3 is unaffected, so he is not cc (CMT is recessive).
His parents are both carriers (Cc), because they have an affected child (individual 4, cc).
An unaffected child of two carriers can be CC (1/4) or Cc (1/2), so the answer is D.

questions.question: What is the probability that a fourth child would be a female with CMT? Options: A 1 in 2, B 1 in 4, C 1 in 8, D 1 in 16.
questions.answer: C: 1 in 8
steps: Both parents are carriers (Cc x Cc), because they have an affected son (individual 4).
Probability of a child with CMT (cc) = 1/4.
Probability that the child is female = 1/2.
Probability of a female with CMT = 1/4 x 1/2 = 1/8, which is option C.

questions.question: In the USA, 5% of the 126 000 people with CMT have a dominant form. Calculate the number with a dominant form.
questions.answer: 6300 people.

questions.question: Draw a genetic diagram for children of a parent without CMT (tt) and a parent with genotype Tt, and indicate whether each child has CMT.
questions.answer: Tt x tt gives 1 Tt (affected with CMT) : 1 tt (unaffected), a 1 : 1 ratio.
steps: The parent without CMT must be tt (recessive, unaffected).
The parent with Tt gives T or t, each with probability 1/2.
The tt parent gives only t, so the children are Tt (1/2) and tt (1/2).
Tt children have the dominant CMT phenotype; tt children are unaffected.

questions.question: Explain why a male with CMT, where the disease is sex-linked on the X chromosome, cannot pass the disease on to his sons.
questions.answer: Sons receive the Y chromosome from their father, not his X, so the X-linked allele cannot be passed to sons.
steps: Males are XY and pass either X or Y to offspring.
A son receives his Y chromosome from his father, not an X chromosome.
So the CMT allele on the father's X can only be passed to daughters.

questions.question: Explain how the CFTR mutation results in reduced gas exchange in the lungs.
questions.answer: The mutation makes mucus thick, which blocks airways and reduces the surface area and ventilation for gas exchange.
steps: The mutated CFTR cannot transport chloride ions, so mucus becomes thick.
Thick mucus blocks the airways and the alveoli.
Less air reaches the alveoli, so the surface area available for diffusion falls.
Less oxygen enters and less carbon dioxide leaves the blood, reducing gas exchange.

questions.question: Calculate the predicted percentage decrease in new cases of cystic fibrosis in the USA, from 964 in 2015 to 839 in 2025.
steps: Percentage decrease = 125 / 964 x 100 = 12.97%.

questions.question: Explain why the number of new cases of cystic fibrosis could fall.
questions.answer: Carrier screening and prenatal testing let at-risk couples avoid affected births, and better awareness reduces the number of new cases.
steps: Carrier screening identifies couples at risk of having a child with CF.
Prenatal testing or PGD can identify affected embryos or foetuses.
Couples can then choose not to continue an affected pregnancy or to avoid conceiving.
Fewer children are born with two recessive alleles, so new cases fall.

questions.question: Devise an investigation to determine whether pre-treatment with drug A is more effective than inhaling a salt solution alone for people with cystic fibrosis, and give reasons for the method.
questions.answer: Use randomised groups given drug A then salt solution, or salt solution alone, in a double-blind controlled trial, measuring mucus clearance and lung function over time.
steps: Recruit people with CF and randomly assign them to two groups to avoid bias.
Group 1: pre-treatment with drug A then salt inhalation; Group 2: salt inhalation only (control).
Use double-blind conditions so neither participants nor researchers know the group.
Measure mucus clearance and FEV1 at regular intervals to see how long the benefit lasts.
Compare the two groups statistically (e.g. chi-squared or t-test) to judge effectiveness.

questions.question: The base labelled Q is thymine. Which is the base labelled P? A adenine, B cytosine, C guanine, D uracil.
questions.answer: A: adenine
steps: P and Q are opposite each other and form one complementary base pair held by hydrogen bonds.
Q is thymine, and thymine pairs only with adenine (A to T, with two hydrogen bonds).
The pair in the diagram shows two dashed lines (two hydrogen bonds), which is consistent with an A-T pair, so P is adenine.

questions.question: Which row of the table identifies the bonds labelled R, S and T in the DNA diagram?
questions.answer: D: R phosphodiester, S covalent, T hydrogen
steps: R is the bond between the deoxyribose sugar and the phosphate group in the sugar-phosphate backbone: a phosphodiester bond.
S joins the sugar to the base: a (glycosidic) covalent bond.
T is the dashed bond between complementary bases: a hydrogen bond.
Only row D has phosphodiester, covalent and hydrogen in that order.

questions.question: Name two types of gene mutation.
questions.answer: Any two of: substitution, insertion, deletion.
steps: A substitution changes one base for another.
An insertion or deletion adds or removes bases and shifts the reading frame.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions that can be made about the mutation rate in the four groups of primates shown in the graph.
questions.answer: Mutation rate falls as the mean age at the start of breeding rises; the highest rate is in prosimians breeding at 4 years, and apes have the lowest rates.
steps: Conclusion 1: there is a negative correlation: the mutation rate falls as the mean age when breeding starts increases, from about 4.4 x 10^-9 at 4 years to about 0.4 x 10^-9 at 30 years.
The fall is steep up to about 10 years, then the rate levels off at about 0.4 to 0.65 x 10^-9 for breeding ages of 10 to 30 years.

Conclusion 2: prosimians that start breeding at about 4 years have the highest mutation rate (about 4.4 x 10^-9 per base pair per year, with a large error bar), while apes, which start breeding latest (19 to 30 years), have the lowest rates.
The points of the four groups overlap, so mutation rate seems to relate to breeding age rather than to which group the primate is in (the error bars on some points also overlap).

questions.question: Explain why most people who have haemophilia are male, given it is inherited like red-green colour blindness.
questions.answer: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive; males have one X, so one recessive allele causes the disorder, while females need two.
steps: The haemophilia gene is on the X chromosome.
Males (XY) have one X and no second allele to mask a recessive allele.
Females (XX) need two recessive alleles, which is much less likely.
Female carriers can pass the allele on but are usually unaffected, so males are more often affected.

questions.question: There were 185 218 people with haemophilia A and 37 998 with haemophilia B. Calculate the ratio of haemophilia A to B to two significant figures.
steps: To two significant figures this is 4.9 : 1.

questions.question: Which is the percentage of the world population with haemophilia A in 2021? A 2.35 x 10^5, B 2.35 x 10^3, C 2.35 x 10^-3, D 2.35 x 10^-5.
steps: As a percentage, multiply by 100: 2.35 x 10^-3 %.

questions.question: Give one reason why the number of people with haemophilia is only an estimate.
questions.answer: Many people with haemophilia are undiagnosed or not reported, so the count is incomplete.
steps: Mild cases may never be diagnosed.
Counts depend on records from clinics and diagnosis, which may be incomplete.

questions.question: Explain how reduced thrombin production in haemophilia affects blood clotting.
questions.answer: Less thrombin means less fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, so fewer fibrin threads form and the clot is weak or slow to form.
steps: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin.
With less thrombin, less fibrin is made.
Fewer fibrin threads trap fewer platelets and red blood cells, so the clot is weak.
Blood takes longer to clot, so bleeding continues for longer.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show one possible structure of a fatty acid side chain of an unsaturated lipid.
questions.answer: Join the four carbons with single bonds and add hydrogen atoms, with one C=C double bond in the chain, for example -CH2-CH=CH-CH3 after the C(=O) group.
steps: An unsaturated fatty acid has at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) in its hydrocarbon chain.
Draw lines between the four carbons, with one double bond between two of them (for example between the 2nd and 3rd carbon).
Add hydrogen atoms so every carbon has four bonds in total: CH2 on the 1st carbon, one H on each carbon of the C=C, and CH3 on the last carbon.
Any valid position for the double bond is acceptable; the chain must not be fully single-bonded (that would be saturated).

questions.question: Calculate the mean rate of increase in the surface of arteries covered in lesions from 16 to 60 months in primates fed saturated lipids (graph 1).
questions.answer: About 1.1 percentage points per month (accept 1.1 to 1.2)
steps: Graph 1, saturated lipids: about 2% of the artery surface covered at 16 months and about 52% at 60 months.
Change = 52 - 2 = 50 percentage points over 60 - 16 = 44 months.
Rate = 50 / 44 = 1.1 % per month (to 2 s.f.).

questions.question: Calculate the ratio of primates with atherosclerosis given saturated lipids to those given unsaturated lipids, at 32 months (graph 2).
steps: Graph 2 at 32 months: about 32% of primates fed saturated lipids have atherosclerosis and about 22% of those fed unsaturated lipids.
Ratio saturated : unsaturated = 32 : 22.
Dividing both by 22 gives 1.45 : 1, which is about 1.5 : 1 (or 16 : 11).

questions.question: Calculate the difference in the area of atheromas in males compared with females given saturated fats (graph 3), in m^2.
steps: Graph 3, saturated lipids after 60 months: males about 0.026 mm^2 and females about 0.004 mm^2.
Convert: 1 mm^2 = 1 000 000 um^2 (10^6, um = micrometre), so 0.022 x 10^6 = 22 000 um^2 (accept about 21 000 to 23 000).

questions.question: Deduce the effects of the two diets (cholesterol with saturated lipids, or with unsaturated lipids) on lesions, atherosclerosis and atheromas in the coronary arteries, using the graphs.
questions.answer: Saturated lipids cause more lesions, more atherosclerosis and larger atheromas than unsaturated lipids, especially after 32 months; lesions and atheromas also appear in unsaturated groups.
steps: Lesions (graph 1): both diets increase the percentage of artery surface covered with age; at 16 and 32 months the diets are similar (2 v 4% and 18 v 16%), but at 60 months saturated lipids give far more (about 52% v 38%).
Atherosclerosis (graph 2): more primates have atherosclerosis on saturated lipids at every age (about 18 v 12% at 16 months, 32 v 22% at 32 months, 56 v 20% at 60 months).
On saturated lipids the percentage with atherosclerosis keeps rising, but on unsaturated lipids it levels off at about 20% after 32 months.

Atheromas (graph 3): after 60 months the area is much bigger on saturated lipids (males about 0.026 mm^2 v 0.007 mm^2 on unsaturated) and females have none or very small ones (about 0.004 mm^2 and 0.0 mm^2).
Males develop bigger atheromas than females on both diets, so sex also affects development; the error bars for males on saturated lipids are large.

Overall, saturated lipids (with cholesterol) cause more severe disease than unsaturated lipids, but unsaturated lipids with cholesterol still produce some lesions, so they do not prevent them completely.

questions.question: Discuss the ethical issues relating to the use of primates and other animals in investigations such as this one.
questions.answer: Animal suffering and welfare must be weighed against the scientific benefit, and the 3Rs (replace, reduce, refine) should be followed.
steps: Primates can suffer, so welfare and pain must be minimised.
The benefit of the knowledge must justify causing harm to the animals.
Researchers should use the 3Rs: replace animals, reduce numbers, and refine methods.
Primates are closely related to humans, so their use raises particular concern.

questions.question: Describe how substitution and insertion or deletion mutations affect the DNA base sequence of a gene.
questions.answer: A substitution replaces one base with another; an insertion or deletion adds or removes bases, shifting the reading frame.
steps: A substitution changes one base, so only one codon may change.
An insertion adds a base and a deletion removes one.
Both shift the reading frame, so all later codons are changed.

questions.question: Explain why these animals can survive with more substitution mutations than insertion and deletion mutations.
questions.answer: Substitutions often change only one codon and may code for the same amino acid, but insertions and deletions shift the reading frame and disrupt every later codon.
steps: Because the genetic code is degenerate, a substitution may not change the amino acid at all.
Even when it does, only one amino acid is changed, so the protein may still work.
An insertion or deletion shifts the reading frame and changes all later codons.
This usually produces a non-functional protein, which is more harmful.

questions.question: Suggest which set of data is the most valid and give a reason for your answer.
questions.answer: Mouse: it has the largest sample size (10 animals), so its data are less affected by anomalies and are more reliable.
steps: Validity and reliability of data increase with sample size.
The table shows 10 mice sampled compared with 3 naked mole rats, 3 dogs and 8 humans.
A larger sample reduces the effect of anomalous results, so the mouse data are the most valid.

questions.question: Calculate the mean mutation rate for the mouse from the graph, drawing a line of best fit.
questions.answer: About 800 mutations per cell per year (accept 700 to 900)
steps: Draw a straight line of best fit through the mouse points, starting at the origin, with about equal numbers of points on each side.
Mean number of mutations per cell: about 540 at 0.6 years, 790 at 1.0, 1100 at 1.4 and 1560 at 2.0 years.
The line passes through about (2.0, 1600), so gradient = 1600 / 2.0 = 800 mutations per cell per year.
The gradient of the line is the mean mutation rate.

questions.question: Describe three conclusions that can be made from the graphs of mutations per cell during the lifespans of four animals.
questions.answer: Mutations per cell increase with age in all four species; the rate differs between species (mouse fastest, human slowest); short-lived animals accumulate mutations faster than long-lived ones.
steps: Conclusion 1: in all four species the number of mutations per cell increases with age (positive correlation).

Conclusion 2: the rate of increase differs between species: the mouse gains about 800 mutations per year, the naked mole rat about 100, the dog about 230 and the human only about 50 (rough estimates from the graphs).
Conclusion 3: the species with shorter lifespans (mouse, 2 years) have much higher mutation rates than those with long lifespans (human, 80 years).

Other acceptable points: humans accumulate the most mutations in total (up to about 4000 per cell), and there is wide variation between individuals of the same age, especially in older mice and humans.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons for the differences in the number of mutations per cell between the species.
questions.answer: Longer-lived or larger animals undergo more cell divisions, and higher metabolic rates produce more DNA-damaging molecules, so more mutations arise.
steps: Mutations arise mainly from errors in DNA replication during cell division.
Animals with longer lifespans or more cell divisions have more chances for errors.
A higher metabolic rate produces more reactive oxygen species that damage DNA.

questions.question: Explain why a safe but effective dose of warfarin needs to be given to a patient.
questions.answer: Too little warfarin fails to prevent clotting, while too much causes dangerous bleeding, so the dose must be in a narrow safe range.
steps: Warfarin is an anticoagulant that reduces blood clotting.
Too low a dose may not prevent harmful clots (e.g. thrombosis).
Too high a dose may cause serious bleeding.

questions.question: Describe the role of mRNA in the production of enzymes.
questions.answer: mRNA is a copy of the gene's base sequence that carries the code from the nucleus to ribosomes, where the polypeptide enzyme is made.
steps: The gene is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus.
mRNA carries the codons out of the nucleus to a ribosome.
At the ribosome, each codon is matched to a tRNA carrying an amino acid, forming the enzyme.

questions.question: Discuss the possible use of pharmacogenomics in selecting appropriate warfarin doses for individual patients, using the information on genes M and V.
questions.answer: Testing the alleles of gene M (slow breakdown) and gene V (less mRNA) lets doctors adjust doses for each patient, improving safety, though testing has cost and ethical issues.
steps: Pharmacogenomics uses a patient's genetic profile to predict drug response.
Patients with slow-breakdown alleles of gene M break warfarin down slowly, so they need lower doses.
Gene V variants reduce mRNA and enzyme V, which changes how strongly warfarin acts.
Using genetic screening can reduce bleeding and clotting events, but costs and privacy must be considered.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term cancer.
questions.answer: A disease in which cells divide uncontrollably by mitosis, forming a tumour that can invade other tissues.
steps: Cancer cells divide uncontrollably because the control of the cell cycle is lost.
The mass of cells forms a tumour.
Cancer cells can invade and spread to other parts of the body.

questions.question: Explain how a substitution mutation could result in collagen that lacks strength.
questions.answer: One base change alters a codon, changing an amino acid in collagen; this disrupts the triple helix structure and the cross-links, so the collagen is weaker.
steps: A substitution changes one base, so one codon is changed.
The codon now codes for a different amino acid in the collagen chain.
This changes the primary structure and so the way collagen chains fold into a triple helix.
A poorly formed triple helix or cross-links make the collagen lack strength.

questions.question: Determine the probability that a child inherits OI if one parent has OI and is heterozygous and the other is homozygous recessive, using a genetic diagram.
questions.answer: 1/2 (0.5): offspring are Dd (affected with OI) or dd (unaffected), in equal numbers.
steps: OI is dominant: the parent with OI is Dd, and the other parent is dd.
The Dd parent gives D or d (each 1/2); the dd parent gives only d.
Offspring: Dd (affected with OI) and dd (unaffected), each with probability 1/2.
So the probability that a child inherits OI is 1/2 (0.5).

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of PGD and prenatal testing for couples at risk of having a child with OI, using the diagram of testing types.
questions.answer: PGD avoids termination but needs IVF; NIPT and CVS give early results, with CVS and amniocentesis being invasive and risking miscarriage; ultrasound and cordocentesis are late and less specific or riskier.
steps: PGD (before implantation): advantage: only embryos without the OI allele are implanted, so no termination of pregnancy; disadvantages: needs IVF, which is expensive, has a lower success rate and raises the ethical issue of discarding embryos.

NIPT (7 to 10 weeks): advantage: non-invasive (only a blood sample), no risk of miscarriage and the earliest result; disadvantages: it tests fetal DNA in the mother's blood so may not be fully diagnostic, and a positive result usually needs confirming.
Chorionic villus sampling (10 to 12 weeks): advantage: early and gives a direct DNA diagnosis; disadvantage: invasive, with a small risk of miscarriage.
Amniocentesis (15 to 20 weeks): advantage: gives a reliable DNA diagnosis; disadvantages: invasive with a risk of miscarriage, and the late result means any termination is later and more distressing.
Ultrasound (after 20 weeks) is non-invasive but late and cannot show the genotype, only abnormalities; cordocentesis (22 to 24 weeks) is very late and carries the highest risk.

General points: because OI is dominant, a heterozygous parent has a 50% chance of passing it on, so testing is informative; false results, cost and ethical objections to termination or embryo selection should be weighed.
